h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to identify which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts can be cut off from the outcome by other settings. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current value in the parent, since replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts and filling an empty or harmful slot helps, and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, which shrink its effect. When finding flaws, replace any hypothesis whose direction could plausibly reverse because of a competing effect, or whose mechanism relies on partial redundancy between different parts. Ensure varied edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed node 1 is dead, so an upgrade on edge 1->2 has almost no effect.
Edge 1->3 reads from the disconnected node 1, so upgrading its op has almost no effect.
With node 1 dead, a conv on edge 1->3 contributes nothing, so the edit's benefit vanishes.
With node 1 dead, a skip on edge 1->2 carries no signal, so its usual benefit disappears.
An empty first edge disconnects node 1 and its downstream edges, so a strong conv there restores them.
Deleting a strong direct edge costs more than deleting a weak one.
Removing a strong conv from the first edge, which gates edges 2 and 4, hurts far more than removing a weak op.
Downgrading a strong conv to a parameter-free skip loses capacity.
Removing a strong conv from edge 1->3 costs more than removing a weak op.
Removing a strong conv from edge 1->2 costs more than removing a weak op.
